articles.title: Karson, keep the two stops. Fix everything that made you need them.
articles.dek: Sunyshore held Blackthorn to 17 rushing yards and still needed two late defensive answers. Mara Voss sees an excellent front—and a warning behind it.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I would hang the final two defensive answers in Sunyshore's meeting room. I would also put the 368 passing yards right beside them, in lettering large enough to ruin everybody's breakfast. Karson Jones has an 8–2 team because his defense made the necessary plays against Blackthorn. That is a reason to trust the Starseekers under pressure. It is a terrible reason to stop asking how much pressure they volunteered to absorb.

At 2:20 of the fourth quarter, Marowak sacked Hatterene on the two-point attempt that could have tied the game. At 1:14, Serp Gardener stopped Seadra after nine yards on fourth-and-eleven. Sunyshore won 21–20. Those are different problems solved by different defenders: get to the passer before the try develops, then make a tackle before the receiver reaches the sticks. Both deserve to be remembered exactly, without being melted into a vague compliment about wanting it more.

The final possession is the better teaching sequence. Exploud caught an eleven-yard pass to start it. Furret then lost a yard running up the middle against Don Philliams. Hatterene missed deep left, Ash Rothington broke up the deep-right throw, and Serp Gardener finished the fourth-down play two yards short. Sunyshore made Blackthorn play the entire series. Nobody needed a spectacular interception to end it. A failed run, two unsuccessful passes and a disciplined tackle did the work.

I like that. I particularly like the tackle. We spend so much time celebrating the ball in the air that a defender who understands where the first down lives can disappear from the discussion. Seadra caught the pass. Serp Gardener still won the down. There is no contradiction in those two facts, and there should be no confusion about which one mattered with a one-point lead.

But go back to the larger afternoon. Hatterene completed 28 of 42 passes for 368 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. Sawsbuck caught six for 142. Exploud caught ten of eleven targets for 94. That is sustained access to a defense, not a couple of freak completions we can wave away while admiring the final scoreboard. The Dragons gained 385 total yards and sixteen first downs. Sunyshore gave itself too many difficult conversations.

The ground defense was excellent. Blackthorn managed seventeen yards on thirteen rushing attempts. Furret had twenty-one on eight carries; the remaining attempts pulled the team total down. Jones's front made running a poor answer for most of the game. Sunyshore has allowed only 365 rushing yards through ten games, so this was consistent with an established strength. I am not asking the Starseekers to abandon that strength. I am asking them to stop treating it as the solution to every question.

Look at the distribution. Exploud's ten receptions kept producing manageable gains, while Sawsbuck supplied the larger chunks. If you only worry about the deep receiver, the underneath catches can extend a drive. If you only squeeze the underneath work, the larger completion changes the field. I cannot tell you the private instructions on any defender's wristband. I can tell you that Blackthorn found productive answers at more than one depth and that those answers survived well into the fourth quarter.

The offense gave the defense considerable help, then less of it. FLOAT SZN ran for 146 yards and two touchdowns on twelve carries. The seventy-yard run up the middle with thirty-seven seconds left in the second quarter was the kind of play that can make an entire game plan look wiser than it felt one snap earlier. He had lost a fumble on Sunyshore's opening play. Jones kept getting him involved, and the back answered. That part of the afternoon deserves applause without a footnote.

"I wanted the next carry to be useful to everybody," FLOAT SZN said. "The line didn't stop working because I lost one. I couldn't either." That is the right-sized answer. A seventy-yard touchdown makes an excellent apology. The more useful part is continuing to do the job after the mistake, because nobody gets to schedule when the long run arrives.

After Jolt Vick's three-yard touchdown catch made the lead 21–7 in the third quarter, the Starseekers never scored again. They finished two-for-eight on third down and punted five times. Blackthorn scored twice in the fourth. Even after the failed tying try, Sunyshore could not finish the game with its offense: an eleven-yard run earned a first down, but an incompletion, a three-yard run and a five-yard run brought another punt. The defense had to go back out and solve the problem again.

That is the part I would put on Jones's desk. There is a perfectly understandable temptation to describe every narrow road win as playoff preparation. Sometimes it is. Sometimes your defense is practicing emergency repairs because your offense has stopped making first downs. DeZhaun Watzon protected the ball, throwing no interceptions, but 175 passing yards and two third-down conversions left little room for a quiet finish. The running game's spectacular moment did not supply an endless supply of possessions.

"We made the stops we needed," Jones said. "I'd rather learn from a win, but the last series doesn't erase the ones before it." Good. Keep that sentence. The coach does not need to apologize for beating an 8–2 opponent on the road, and I am not asking him to. I want the corrections to receive the same attention as the relief. A contender should be capable of celebrating and studying in the same building.

Eterna comes next. The Thorns just lost 38–0, which makes them an easy opponent to underestimate and a useful test of Sunyshore's patience. The Starseekers do not need to manufacture another dramatic fourth quarter to prove they can win one. They need to turn their defensive advantage into enough ordinary offensive possessions that the final drive belongs to their own kneeling quarterback. If Eterna struggles to move the ball, keep making it struggle; do not hand it a shorter route back into the game.

I believe in this defense's ability to make a hard stop. Marowak and Serp Gardener gave me two very good reasons. I also believe Jones has enough evidence to demand a cleaner afternoon. Freeze the last fourth-down catch on the screen: Seadra has the ball, Serp Gardener has the tackle, and the first-down line is still two yards away. Keep that frame. Then rewind.

articles.title: Petalburg would like its lead back in the conversation
articles.dek: Rustboro gets the unbeaten visitor. Petalburg has the division lead. Ellis Quill thinks the distinction deserves a little attention.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: There is a pleasant kind of anonymity available to a team that keeps winning while someone else gets the interesting visitor. Petalburg is 7–3, leading Hoenn West, and preparing for Sootopolis. Rustboro is 6–4 and preparing for unbeaten Mossdeep. I know which game people will talk about first. I would like to spend a few minutes with the team that is already in front.

Norman's Pride won 24–17 at Pewter without producing a passing line anyone will frame. Iron Valiant completed fourteen of twenty-five throws for 115 yards. There were two touchdowns and no interceptions, which is a much better description of his afternoon than the yardage alone. Petalburg rushed for 145 yards, recovered a fumble and made the long field goal that left the home team with too much to do. The victory was assembled from useful pieces.

Oinkologne supplied two of the most useful. On fourth-and-two in the third quarter, he caught a two-yard touchdown pass. Early in the fourth, he ran up the middle for a one-yard score. A receiving touchdown of two yards and a rushing touchdown of one are not likely to win a contest for the week's most beautiful highlights. They were, however, exactly the distances Petalburg needed. I have a soft spot for players who decline to make a simple assignment sound inadequate.

"If it's two yards, I'll take two," Oinkologne said. "We can admire the long ones after we finish the short ones." There is a brave little impatience in that answer. He carried fifteen times for seventy yards, so the afternoon was not all short work. But those two scoring plays explain the Pride's approach better than a grand statement about identity ever could. Find the job, finish the job, let someone else count the style points.

The fourth-down touchdown was followed almost immediately by Pewter's fumble. Sandslash recovered it for Petalburg. It is tempting to treat those moments as luck lining up politely for the visitors, but a team has to convert the opening. The Pride turned the next possession into Oinkologne's one-yard score. In a game decided by seven points, the ability to make the next opportunity useful was the difference between controlling the afternoon and merely participating in it.

Pewter still made the finish uncomfortable. There was an eight-yard fourth-down touchdown pass to Marowak, and later a two-yard fourth-down scoring pass to Cranidos with eighteen seconds remaining. Before that last drive, Sunflora had made a fifty-three-yard field goal at 1:56. That kick gave Petalburg a fourteen-point cushion. By the time Cranidos scored, the Rockers needed an onside recovery as well as another touchdown. Cradily recovered the kick for the Pride. Iron Valiant took a knee.

I mention the sequence because narrow final scores can flatten the story. Petalburg did not spend the final eighteen seconds trying to prevent one ordinary possession from becoming a tying touchdown. The Pride had already made Pewter spend most of the remaining time on its first necessary score. The onside kick was a real danger, and Cradily still had to secure it. But the long field goal had changed the demands on the opponent. That is what a good kick buys.

"You don't want to need every one of those details," Norman said. "You do want everyone to understand that their detail counts." He has a team with a plus-thirty-four point differential, not the sort of margin that encourages leisurely afternoons. Petalburg has scored 186 points and allowed 152. Seven wins have come from that narrower space. I would be careful about assuming the Pride can always live there, and equally careful about dismissing a team that has repeatedly found a way through it.

The comparison with Rustboro is interesting because the Stone have produced more noise in fewer winning afternoons. Their most recent game was a 41–38 victory over Cinnabar before the Week 11 bye. They have scored 205 points and allowed 174, almost the same overall differential as Petalburg despite the different shape of the results. Rustboro can make a game feel open and urgent. Petalburg just won with 115 passing yards and a very important fifty-three-yard kick. Both routes count.

Dewford is also 6–4 after winning 16–10 at Celadon. That makes the division lead a live responsibility rather than a comfortable possession. Petalburg cannot outsource its Week 12 work to Mossdeep, however useful a Rustboro defeat might look from a distance. Sootopolis has four wins and just lost at Fuchsia. The Surge have also shown they can put together a clean passing game when allowed to settle. Norman's team needs to win its own afternoon before admiring the result from Rustboro.

I resist calling this a statement game for the Pride. Everything is a statement game once we run out of more specific language. Petalburg's statement is the record it has already built. Week 12 is an opportunity to preserve a one-game lead over two pursuers and to keep a division winner's route through the postseason within its own reach. That is plenty. We do not need to pretend a comfortable spot has been secured, or that the next loss would erase ten weeks of work.

Iron Valiant was characteristically economical about the attention. "The backs gave us places to go," he said. "The line kept giving us another down. I'm happy if the numbers tell that part too." His two touchdown passes traveled to Delcatty and Oinkologne for short scores. There is no need to inflate them into feats they were not. The quarterback put the ball where a small gain could become six points. Some afternoons, that is the whole brief.

The Pride's lead also gives the next several weeks a different emotional rhythm. Chasing teams can spend a good deal of time imagining what one win might repair. A team in front has to keep doing the unglamorous work that made the lead possible. Norman will not get to protect first place with an explanation of why Rustboro's matchup received more attention. He gets Sootopolis, a fresh opening kickoff, and the same obligation to make the next manageable play.

I will watch Mossdeep at Rustboro with everybody else. It deserves the attention. I will also keep an eye on Petalburg, because the Hoenn West standings still begin with the Pride. Last week their final necessary touch belonged to Cradily on an onside kick. A player secured the ball, a quarterback knelt, and the division leader went home with its seventh win.

articles.title: Koga, do not let 2–9 become an excuse
articles.dek: Fuchsia finally paired Empoleon’s passing with protection and a defense that finished. Dorian Pike demands that the Shadows remember the recipe.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Koga, I have a modest request. Keep the tape. Label it clearly. Put it somewhere nobody can mistake it for a souvenir from a season that has already disappointed them. Fuchsia beat Sootopolis 24–14, and for once the Shadows gave their quarterback an afternoon in which every completed pass did not appear to be negotiating with disaster. Empoleon threw for 283 yards. He took no sacks. He threw no interceptions. I would like those three facts to become acquainted with one another permanently.

Yes, Fuchsia is 2–9. I can read the standings. I have been reading them while this team found creative ways to make good passing yardage feel like an apology. Empoleon now has 2,427 passing yards. A quarterback can accumulate a large number while his team loses; nobody needs another seminar on that point. What matters is whether the rest of the operation gives those yards somewhere useful to go. This week, it did.

The Shadows gained 382 total yards, made seventeen first downs and allowed only six. They held the opposing ground game to thirty yards on eleven attempts. They recorded three sacks and an interception. They won by ten despite missing two field goals and losing a fumble. This was not a perfect performance that briefly appeared from a more successful team's wardrobe. It was an imperfect performance with enough competent football underneath it to survive its own mistakes.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: a 2–9 team still has standards to meet. The record does not issue an exemption. It makes the demand more urgent. If Koga can get this protection, this level of quarterback efficiency and this much defensive resistance in the same game, then I want to know why the next opponent should be allowed to treat Fuchsia as a pleasant stop on the schedule. I am finished congratulating opponents for showing up.

Start with Vivillon. Six catches, 122 yards, two touchdowns. There was also a fumble after a twenty-five-yard catch late in the second quarter. That detail stays in the column. I am not polishing the evidence until it reflects a nicer team. The important response came after halftime: a twenty-nine-yard touchdown catch, then a five-yard touchdown catch, both to the left. Fuchsia continued to throw to a player who could hurt the defense. The player rewarded the decision.

"I wanted another chance with the ball," Vivillon said. "Two touchdowns felt a lot better than spending the whole evening talking about the one I dropped." Good. Enjoy them. Then remember that the first mistake did not force the coaching staff to abandon the receiver, and the receiver did not force the quarterback to stop trusting him. A young season can be full of promises. An eleven-game season needs useful responses. Those two catches were useful.

Empoleon completed twenty of twenty-seven passes. Heatmor caught six of seven targets for seventy-seven yards. Gumshoos caught all four of his for thirty-three. The distribution matters because the offense was not reduced to begging one player for another rescue. Vivillon had the largest afternoon, but there were other catches available and other receivers finishing their assignments. A defense asked to respect several productive routes has more work to do than one waiting for the same desperation throw.

The protection deserves its own paragraph, and it is getting one. Zero sacks. I am writing that again because quarterbacks on losing teams are so often discussed as if every dropback happens in a private room. Empoleon had been sacked twenty-four times across the season's recorded totals; none came in this game. Whatever compliments go to the passer should leave enough room for the players who prevented the pocket from becoming an emergency exit. That is a collective achievement.

Fuchsia also ran the ball thirty-one times for ninety-nine yards. Oinkologne supplied eighty-five on twenty-one carries. Bibarel scored from a yard out in the first quarter. I am not going to sell 3.2 yards per team rushing attempt as a revelation. I am going to recognize that the Shadows could keep calling runs without asking the quarterback to solve every down by himself. Bibarel's touchdown was a one-yard answer to a one-yard problem. Those answers have been in short supply.

Now the defense. Cacturne and Sharpedo each sacked the opposing quarterback for seven-yard losses, and Gumshoos added another sack. Seaking intercepted a deep-left throw. Seven passes were swatted away. The opponent completed eleven of twenty-seven attempts and converted two of ten third downs. You can build a winning afternoon around that kind of resistance. You cannot spend the following week acting surprised that resistance was permitted.

The ending was even better than the big defensive totals. After Fuchsia missed a forty-yard field goal at 1:58, the opponent still had a small opening. A nine-yard completion created second-and-one. Then came an incompletion, a run for no gain stopped by Sharpedo, and a fourth-down run that lost a yard to Cacturne. At 1:46, Empoleon began taking knees. The defense closed the door after the kicker had failed to do it. That is what a team is supposed to be for.

"We didn't have to ask for the ball back," Koga said. "We had to finish the down in front of us." Fine. Keep that answer too. There is a temptation around a losing club to describe every good moment as a preview of next season. I object. There are games left in this season. There are players trying to establish that their work should matter now. Fuchsia's defense did not stop that fourth-down run for the benefit of a future slogan.

Pewter is next, and I expect Fuchsia to arrive with an actual plan to win. That is not a claim that the Shadows have suddenly become a contender. It is a refusal to let nine losses lower the standard for the next opportunity to do something useful. Repeat the protection. Keep multiple receivers involved. Make the opponent earn its third downs. If the field-goal unit leaves points behind, do not allow the rest of the team to use the miss as permission to drift.

Koga, the record is bad. The football does not have to stay bad. Your quarterback finished this game with 283 passing yards and no sacks, and your defense finished it by denying one yard twice. Put those two plays on the first screen at the next meeting. Leave them there long enough for everybody to read the distance.

articles.title: Hatterene takes the next examination: Blackthorn at unbeaten Mt. Silver
articles.dek: The Dragons just threw for 368 yards and lost by one. Now they visit a defense allowing 6.8 points per game, with conference position and the Reds’ perfect record at stake.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Blackthorn should arrive at Mt. Silver convinced it can move the ball. The Dragons should also arrive worried about whether moving it will be enough. Hatterene threw for 368 yards and three touchdowns against Sunyshore, and the result was a 21–20 loss. The next opponent has allowed sixty-eight points all season and none over its last two games. That is a useful way to introduce the Game of the Week: an excellent passer trying to make an unbeaten defense spend more of the afternoon answering questions.

Mt. Silver is 10–0. Blackthorn is 8–2. Both currently lead their divisions, and the Reds hold the first seed in the Kanto–Johto table while the Dragons hold the second. A Blackthorn win would bring the records to 10–1 and 9–2, narrowing the separation to one game. A Reds win would make them 11–0 and leave the Dragons 8–3. Those are substantial consequences without pretending this one result settles the postseason. The remaining schedule still has work for everybody.

My pick is Mt. Silver, 27–20. I expect Blackthorn to score and to force a more demanding game than the Reds' recent shutouts. I also expect Connor McLarren's team to have the broader set of answers when the game stops being comfortable. That distinction begins with the defensive matchup, but it does not end there. Mt. Silver has improved its available quarterback play while waiting on injured players, and now it gets a useful runner back.

The most persuasive part of the Eterna win was the absence of ordinary progress. The Thorns gained eighty-four total yards, made three first downs and went zero-for-eight on third down. Tatsugiri completed eight of nineteen for forty-one passing yards. Mt. Silver recorded one sack, so the defensive result cannot be explained simply as a parade of quarterback hits. Eterna repeatedly failed to turn its opportunities into the next set of downs. Blackthorn must make the Reds defend a different kind of possession.

Hatterene is equipped to try. His season line stands at 221 completions in 302 attempts, 2,510 yards, twenty-four touchdowns and four interceptions. Against Sunyshore, he completed twenty-eight of forty-two without an interception. The Dragons reached 385 total yards and sixteen first downs. Those numbers describe a passing attack that can keep several receiving routes relevant, even when the running game has been reduced to an occasional suggestion. They do not describe an offense that needs to begin again from nothing after one loss.

The receiving distribution is where I would start the matchup. Sawsbuck caught six passes for 142 yards against Sunyshore. Exploud caught ten of eleven targets for ninety-four. One supplied the larger gains; the other kept giving Hatterene a productive answer. Mt. Silver has to prevent those jobs from reinforcing each other. If Exploud's catches repeatedly create manageable downs, the defense cannot treat every apparent passing situation as an invitation to chase the quarterback. If Sawsbuck gets behind it, the cost of an otherwise good series changes immediately.

Blackthorn will make that attempt with fewer available receivers. Ninjask, who caught five passes for eighty-nine yards against the Starseekers, is out two weeks. Grovyle remains out five. Together they have contributed 865 receiving yards this season. Their absence is not a reason to declare Hatterene helpless; it is a reason to ask who will take the next useful target and whether that player can make the Reds respect the same space. Sawsbuck and Exploud have just demonstrated they can produce. They should expect an opponent that has noticed.

The running game needs a less ambitious but equally important repair. Blackthorn managed seventeen yards on thirteen attempts against Sunyshore. Furret gained twenty-one on eight carries, while the rest of the rushing line pulled the total backward. The Dragons do not need to imitate a different offense for an entire afternoon. They do need enough successful early-down runs that Hatterene is not repeatedly asked to manufacture the whole possession through the air. An extra four or five useful yards can change how a third down feels.

The final Blackthorn series against Sunyshore explains that need particularly well. Exploud opened with an eleven-yard catch. Furret then lost a yard up the middle. Two incomplete deep passes followed, and Seadra's nine-yard catch on fourth-and-eleven ended two yards short. That was a perfectly ordinary sequence of small failures after a useful opening. Against Mt. Silver, Clair cannot assume the next possession will arrive in time to repair it. Keeping the run from losing ground matters even when the passing total looks excellent.

Mt. Silver's offense has its own questions, but the recent answers have been encouraging. Tic Thorpe followed his three-touchdown passing game at Canalave with four against Eterna. He completed twenty-three of forty for 252 yards, took no sacks and threw no interceptions in the 38–0 win. The Reds converted six of thirteen third downs and gained 352 yards. They did not need every pass to work because the defense kept returning the game to them, and because useful completions became touchdowns in several different hands.

That last point matters with Gregar Jenings still out one week and Josh Alakazam out eleven. Tony Gyarzalez caught six passes for seventy-four yards against Eterna and scored on a thirty-one-yard catch in the third quarter. Plusico Buress had four catches for sixty-eight and a touchdown. The offense has not been reduced to waiting for one missing player to reappear. Thorpe's season passing sample is still much smaller than Hatterene's, so I am not declaring the quarterback question permanently settled. I am recognizing two consecutive productive games in the job.

Garshawn Lynch now has no remaining injury absence. He has 672 rushing yards on eighty-six carries this season, an important available option even before anybody promises a particular workload. Raticate ran for fifty-two yards against Eterna and Vibrava for forty-eight. McLarren has received useful work from the available backs; Lynch's return offers another way to make Blackthorn defend the ground. The Dragons just allowed FLOAT SZN 146 yards, including a seventy-yard touchdown. Their next answer cannot be merely to hope the long run stays off the schedule.

I will watch the first few ordinary rushing possessions more closely than the first spectacular pass. If Mt. Silver keeps gaining enough on the ground to leave Thorpe with manageable decisions, Blackthorn's defense must solve two problems while its offense is missing two receiving contributors. If the Dragons close those runs down, they can make the Reds' passing game demonstrate its new stability under more demanding conditions. A restored runner matters most when the blockers and the situation let him influence the next down.

Blackthorn's route to winning is clear enough to be credible. Give Hatterene usable possession, involve Exploud early, make Sawsbuck's larger opportunities count, and avoid letting the rushing game put the offense behind schedule. On defense, hold the Reds below 120 rushing yards and make Thorpe finish longer series rather than repeatedly work from short fields. My slate also asks the Dragons to convert at least five third downs. Three-for-ten against Sunyshore left too many useful passing yards stranded between scoring chances.

Mt. Silver's route is to keep the game broad. Make the backs contribute, let Tony Gyarzalez and Plusico Buress give Thorpe different receiving answers, and avoid the turnovers that would let Blackthorn skip the difficult part of moving against this defense. My two published keys are to keep the Dragons below twenty-four points and commit no turnovers. Those are measurable targets, not guarantees. They describe the game I expect: Blackthorn occasionally breaking through, then having to build the next score against a team that refuses to donate the opening.

The panel is divided more sharply than my seven-point margin suggests. Rowan, Mara and Ellis have all picked Blackthorn. Dorian and I have Mt. Silver, a temporary alliance that should not be mistaken for agreement about everything he has said this season. I understand the upset case. Hatterene has the production to make even an excellent defense uncomfortable. I am staying with the Reds because the defense is paired with enough current offensive variety to survive that discomfort.

I do not expect another zero beside the visitor's name. Blackthorn has earned more respect than that, and Hatterene's last game supplied specific reasons to give it. I expect the decisive difference to be a possession on which Mt. Silver can still run, still use the tight end and still ask Thorpe for a manageable throw. Blackthorn has just lost by one while making 368 passing yards useful almost everywhere except the final score. My forecast gives the Dragons twenty points and the Reds twenty-seven.

art.alt: Blackthorn’s Hatterene faces Mt. Silver’s Tic Thorpe beneath a silver mountain.

articles.title: The Stone have more than one answer. Mossdeep will make them use every one.
articles.dek: Rustboro returns rested and healthier after a five-touchdown passing game. Tessa Wren examines how the Stone can test the 10–0 Eclipse—and why she still favors Mossdeep.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Rustboro's most useful argument against Mossdeep's unbeaten record is the one it made before the bye. Porygon-Z threw five touchdown passes in a 41–38 win over Cinnabar. The Stone could already ask opponents to respect their runners; that afternoon supplied another answer. Now the 6–4 hosts get My Way, Son back without a remaining injury absence and welcome a 10–0 opponent whose latest receiving performance made almost every available defensive answer look expensive.

My forecast is Mossdeep, 34–24. The Eclipse have sustained more complete offensive production across the season, and their recent passing creates difficult choices for any opponent. Rustboro has a plausible route to changing the result, however. It begins with making that offense wait, continues through using more than one kind of scoring threat, and depends on refusing to let a good Mossdeep receiver turn several normal possessions into a few seconds of pursuit. The Stone need a full afternoon, not one perfect opening drive.

The standings give the game two different kinds of urgency. Mossdeep is first in Hoenn East and holds the leading seed in the Hoenn–Sinnoh conference table. Rustboro is second in Hoenn West, one game behind 7–3 Petalburg and level on record with 6–4 Dewford. Petalburg hosts Sootopolis while Dewford hosts Lavaridge. A Rustboro win could keep the Stone close or bring them level on wins and losses with the Pride, depending on the other result. A defeat could leave a two-game gap if Petalburg wins. None of those possibilities removes Rustboro's own assignment.

Tyler Scarboro has had a bye to prepare for it. The last Stone game is still worth studying because the passing production came through specific, repeatable opportunities rather than a final total alone. Porygon-Z completed sixteen of twenty-five for 268 yards, five touchdowns and one interception. Gibby Timmy caught touchdown passes of thirty-three, ten and forty-six yards. Gengar supplied a nineteen-yard scoring catch. Rustboro made Cinnabar defend several routes to the end zone, and it did so without allowing a sack.

That performance should change how the Eclipse approach the next game. Calling Rustboro a running team is a useful description of its season totals; it is an incomplete description of its last result. The Stone have 1,608 rushing yards through ten games, six more than Mossdeep. They also just showed that concentrating on the ground can leave Porygon-Z with productive receiving opportunities. Michael Dorrill needs a defense that can contest those opportunities without making the returning backfield a secondary concern.

My Way, Son's availability makes that balance more difficult. He has 693 rushing yards on eighty-eight carries this season. Philly has added 504 on 103, and Watchog 202 on thirty-nine. Those are separate contributors rather than a single workload waiting for one injured player to return. Parasect also has no remaining injury absence. The public availability report gives Scarboro more options; it does not tell us exactly how he will distribute them. I want to see whether those options keep Rustboro out of the obvious passing situations Mossdeep would prefer to create.

The Eclipse's defense has earned respect for more than the team's record. Mossdeep has allowed ninety-seven points and 597 rushing yards through ten games, while recording twenty-seven sacks. At Vermilion, Chandelure was sacked five times for thirty-four yards. Joey Sporeter was one of the central defensive contributors in that 45–21 win. Pressure can make a productive passing plan much less comfortable, especially if the run fails to keep the offense on schedule. Rustboro's sack-free afternoon against Cinnabar is evidence of a useful response, not a promise that every opponent will permit it.

There is also an opening the Stone should take seriously. Marshall Flock remains out four weeks. Vermilion completed seventeen of twenty-four passes for 221 yards and three touchdowns without an interception against Mossdeep. The Volts lost heavily because they could not keep up with the Eclipse's offense, but their passing was productive. Scarboro should study that part without assuming the same throws will be available. A good preview distinguishes a demonstrated vulnerability from an automatic instruction for exploiting it.

The other side of the matchup begins with Accel BeckhmJr. Seven catches, 259 yards, four touchdowns. The scoring receptions at Vermilion covered thirteen, sixty, sixty-six and sixty-nine yards. The last three were recorded to the right, and the sixty-six-yard score followed immediately after Vermilion had cut the deficit to ten. That is why a reasonable Rustboro possession plan can disappear quickly: Mossdeep does not always need a long sequence of first downs to undo several minutes of the opponent's work.

The season numbers make it harder to dismiss the performance as an isolated event. Accel has forty-five catches for 1,035 yards and seventeen touchdowns in nine appearances. Dram Marino has completed 176 of 257 throws for 2,640 yards, thirty-one touchdowns and three interceptions. Those totals do not mean the next deep pass must work. They mean Rustboro's defense has to treat the possibility as a recurring part of the assignment, even after it has played several good snaps in a row.

Rustboro's answer cannot stop with Accel, because Gronkaludon caught six passes for seventy yards at Vermilion and has fifty catches for 581 yards this season. Taking away the largest receiving play matters. Leaving an easy succession of smaller completions can still keep the defense on the field and move Mossdeep toward the same scoring opportunity. I would judge the Stone's coverage by whether Marino has to work through genuinely difficult decisions, rather than by whether one famous name has been quiet for a quarter.

Ninjaskamara makes the problem broader again. He ran for ninety-one yards and two touchdowns against Vermilion, scoring from eight and seven yards. For the season he has 1,122 rushing yards and twenty rushing touchdowns, plus fifteen catches for 306 yards and three more scores. Rustboro cannot simply move every available answer toward the deepest receiver and trust the rest to happen behind it. The Eclipse can reach the end zone through a back who has repeatedly finished shorter opportunities as well as a receiver who has made long ones feel brief.

That does not make Mossdeep invulnerable. Marino threw an interception late in the third quarter at Vermilion. The Eclipse finished with thirteen first downs despite 459 total yards, a reminder that this particular win leaned heavily on the largest completions. Rustboro can make the next game less comfortable by preventing those immediate scores and demanding more successful plays in each series. One takeaway would help; building the entire plan around an expected giveaway would be wishful thinking against a quarterback with only three interceptions all season.

The Stone's own defense must also improve on the ending of its Cinnabar win. Rustboro allowed twenty-eight fourth-quarter points, including a ninety-seven-yard kickoff return. Gholdengo finished with 325 passing yards. The offense kept finding another answer, but a ten-point forecast against Mossdeep cannot assume that every defensive failure will be repaid with a touchdown on the next possession. Special teams matter here too. A team trying to keep Marino off the field cannot give away a different kind of rapid score while congratulating itself on the possession count.

My published Rustboro keys are at least 140 rushing yards and fewer than four Mossdeep offensive touchdowns. The first asks the Stone to make their healthier backfield a real part of the contest. The second asks the defense to change the scale of the afternoon. Holding the Eclipse to three offensive touchdowns would not guarantee a win, particularly if kicks or returns become decisive. It would give Rustboro's own passing and running enough space to matter without demanding another forty-one-point performance.

For Mossdeep, the slate asks for at least 350 total yards and no more than one turnover. I expect Marino to find enough receiving work even if Accel does not repeat the extraordinary Vermilion line. Gronkaludon and Ninjaskamara make that forecast less dependent on one player. Defensively, the Eclipse need to make Rustboro earn its passing chances by first resisting the runners. If the Stone can use My Way, Son to produce manageable downs and then find Gibby Timmy beyond them, the game becomes a much more uncomfortable exchange.

Four panelists favor Mossdeep. Dorian has Rustboro winning 38–21, a score that gives him ample room for either a triumphant column or a change of subject. His underlying case is recognizable: the Stone are rested, healthier and coming off a five-touchdown passing game; the Eclipse just conceded three passing touchdowns. My disagreement is about how often Rustboro can make all those advantages work while defending Mossdeep's several scoring threats. The longer season of evidence points me toward the visitors.

I will watch the first ordinary Rustboro third down almost as closely as the first Marino deep throw. If the Stone are facing a manageable distance because the runners have done useful work, Porygon-Z can keep more of his recent answers available. If they are repeatedly trying to recover from lost yards, Mossdeep's pressure can turn the game toward its preferred rhythm. Rustboro has earned a serious preview. Mossdeep has earned the forecast: thirty-four points to twenty-four, with the Stone making the unbeaten visitors use more than one answer.

articles.title: Week 12: unbeaten teams, uncomfortable road tests, and thirty keys
articles.dek: Blackthorn visits Mt. Silver, Mossdeep goes to Rustboro, and Saffron visits a rested Cinnabar. Tessa Wren previews all fifteen games before the panel makes seventy-five calls.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Rowan won Week 11 at 10–4. I went 9–5, Mara 8–6, Ellis 7–7 and Dorian 5–9. Mara collected six shared closest-score bonuses, Ellis five, Rowan three, and Dorian and I two apiece. The bonuses remain a separate measure of score accuracy; they do not rescue a wrong winner.

My Mossdeep key asked for twenty completions. Dram Marino needed sixteen to throw for 354 yards and four touchdowns. Sunyshore was closer to my actual argument: I asked for at least 120 rushing yards, and FLOAT SZN supplied 146 by himself. Blackthorn completed twenty-eight of forty-two passes, below my seventy-percent target, and lost by one. The results keep the forecasts honest. They also show why a good winner pick does not certify every proposed route to it.

Week 12 has fifteen games, with Canalave and Hearthome on byes. Blackthorn at Mt. Silver is my Game of the Week; Mossdeep at Rustboro receives its own feature as well. Saffron at Cinnabar could demand just as much attention by the finish. Below are thirty measurable keys and fifteen scorelines. The panel records use the predictions saved before each game, with season coverage beginning in Week 5.

matchups.matchup: Vermilion brings its passing response to a rested rival
matchups.analysis: Chandelure threw three touchdowns without an interception against Mossdeep. That would normally be a useful beginning to a winning report; the Volts allowed forty-five points. Vermilion is now 6–4 and minus-thirty, while Viridian returns at 4–6 after its bye. I favor the visitors narrowly because their quarterback supplied a credible response even against an unbeaten opponent. The Titans need to make that response less comfortable and give their defense more scoring support than the seven points they produced at Petalburg. Tentacruel and Delcatty remain absent for Vermilion; Sneasel remains out for Viridian. Neither secondary receives a clean bill of health just because the matchup is more manageable. The team that protects its passer should find enough opportunities to make this close.
matchups.awayKey: Complete at least sixty percent of passes and lose no more than one turnover.
matchups.homeKey: Score at least two passing touchdowns and hold Vermilion below ninety rushing yards.

matchups.matchup: Fuchsia has finally finished a passing argument
matchups.analysis: Empoleon went twenty-for-twenty-seven for 283 yards and two touchdowns in the Shadows' 24–14 win over Sootopolis. Vivillon caught both scoring passes. Fuchsia is still 2–9; one afternoon has not repaired the season. It has supplied a reason to pick the Shadows against a 4–6 Pewter side that allowed Petalburg twenty-four points. Wyrdeer threw two touchdowns of his own, so the Rockers have a practical answer beyond waiting for the defense to rescue them. Both teams remain depleted at cornerback. I give Fuchsia a small edge because its latest passing performance offered more sustained production, supported by eighty-five Oinkologne rushing yards. Brock's route is to turn that apparent balance into long drives that finish without touchdowns.
matchups.awayKey: Gain at least 250 passing yards and score on three possessions.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Fuchsia below one hundred rushing yards and commit no turnovers.

matchups.matchup: Cerulean needs the last few yards as much as the first three hundred
matchups.analysis: Farigiraf threw for 321 yards and Cerulean still lost 22–21 to Lavaridge. This week's assignment should be more forgiving, but the 4–6 Tide have wasted enough passing movement to earn skepticism. Celadon fell to 2–9 after a 16–10 loss to Dewford, with Vanillish completing ten of twenty-nine for 118 yards and two interceptions. Gholdengo now carries a nine-week absence on the Bloom's injury list. I expect Cerulean's passing game to create more chances than the home offense can match. Erika can overturn that forecast by leaning on Seaking, shortening the game and making Farigiraf pay for another interception. The Tide need useful finishes. Nobody awards a separate victory for crossing the three-hundred-yard mark.
matchups.awayKey: Score at least three offensive touchdowns and throw no interceptions.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least one hundred yards and force two turnovers.

matchups.matchup: Saffron’s flood of points meets Cinnabar’s rested response
matchups.analysis: Dam Skattebo ran for 156 yards and five touchdowns while Archam Manning threw for 329 in Saffron's 52–0 win over Fortree. Cinnabar's last appearance produced thirty-eight points and a loss at Rustboro. The 8–2 Psi Corps have allowed seventy points all season; the 7–3 Blaze are more likely than Fortree to make that defense work. I take Saffron by three because its most recent attack could win through both its quarterback and its back. Verrick Brooks and Ninetales remain out one week, and Emmitt Smoth joins the injury list for two. Blaine should test those absences with Gholdengo's passing, but the Blaze also need to prevent another receiver from taking over the way Gibby Timmy did before the bye. Expect offense on both sides, with Saffron's stronger defensive record supplying the deciding possession.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for at least 120 yards and allow no more than two sacks.
matchups.homeKey: Throw at least three touchdown passes and hold Saffron below thirty points.

matchups.matchup: Mahogany’s good differential has stopped making the argument for it
matchups.analysis: Mahogany is 3–6–1 after losing 20–13 to Pastoria. Porygon-Z completed eight of eighteen for 114 yards; the Frost's positive differential has narrowed to seven. Azalea is 4–7 after losing 13–10 to Oreburgh, with seventy-five passing yards from Drampa. Neither attack has earned much confidence. I give the visitors a modest edge because Exploud's sixty-one rushing yards at least supplied a way to ease the passing burden. Doduo remains absent for Azalea, while Mahogany still misses Kricketune. Bugsy can win if the Swarm turn the game into repeated short fields. Pryce needs to make ordinary possessions productive enough that his team stops depending on its earlier, better afternoons to explain the present record.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for at least ninety yards and finish three scoring drives.
matchups.homeKey: Force two turnovers and hold Mahogany below two hundred passing yards.

matchups.matchup: Game of the Week: Blackthorn gets the unbeaten Reds next
matchups.analysis: The Dragons threw for 368 yards and lost 21–20 to Sunyshore. Now an 8–2 team travels to 10–0 Mt. Silver, which has won its last two games by a combined 72–0. Tic Thorpe threw four touchdowns against Eterna; Hatterene threw three against the Starseekers. The difference I expect is how much help each passer receives. Sunyshore's FLOAT SZN ran for 146 yards at Blackthorn, while the Reds' defense held Eterna's entire passing game to forty-one. Mt. Silver has Garshawn Lynch back without a remaining injury absence, although Gregar Jenings remains out one week. Blackthorn loses Ninjask for two weeks alongside Grovyle's five-week absence. Clair can still attack through Sawsbuck and Exploud. I favor the Reds because their defense is better positioned to make an excellent quarterback's afternoon merely useful instead of decisive.
matchups.awayKey: Allow fewer than 120 rushing yards and convert at least five third downs.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Blackthorn below twenty-four points and commit no turnovers.

matchups.matchup: Violet’s fourth straight win earns a harder look
matchups.analysis: Violet beat Hearthome 24–6, with Iron Jugulis completing twenty-four of thirty-six for 231 yards and accounting for three touchdowns. The Falcons are 6–4 after four straight wins. Olivine is 5–5 after a 6–3 loss to Canalave, with 137 passing yards and another injury at tight end: Gogoat is out two weeks alongside Veluza's four. I prefer Violet because its recent defensive reliability now has a more useful scoring partner. The Ironclads can keep this close by making the Falcons sustain long possessions instead of giving Samurott easy receiving volume. Jasmine also needs more than three points. A low-scoring game helps a limited offense only while the other team agrees to remain equally limited.
matchups.awayKey: Score touchdowns on at least two possessions and allow no more than one passing touchdown.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least ninety yards and convert four third downs.

matchups.matchup: Lavender’s recovery travels with fewer available receivers
matchups.analysis: Mr. Clanky recovered from a ninety-six-yard game with 223 passing yards and three total touchdowns in Lavender's 31–14 win over Veilstone. Diggersby added 101 rushing yards and two touchdowns of his own. The Wails reached 5–5, but People Eater is now out six weeks and Beedrill one. Cianwood has won two straight to reach 4–7, with Bibarel rushing for 121 yards against Snowpoint while Swampert handled the passing. I favor Lavender narrowly because its restored passing gives it a second route to points. That route must survive the receiving absences. The Crushers can win by making Bibarel the center of the afternoon and forcing Travis Scarboro's available receivers to keep converting without their usual company.
matchups.awayKey: Complete at least eighteen passes and lose no more than one turnover.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least 130 yards and hold Lavender below twenty-one points.

matchups.matchup: Mossdeep’s unbeaten offense meets the rested Stone
matchups.analysis: Mossdeep is 10–0 after a 45–21 win in which Accel BeckhmJr caught seven passes for 259 yards and all four Dram Marino touchdown throws. Rustboro returns at 6–4 after its 41–38 win over Cinnabar and a bye. Porygon-Z threw five touchdowns in that game, so describing the Stone only through their runners would miss the most recent evidence. My Way, Son and Parasect now have no remaining injury absence; Marshall Flock remains out four weeks for the Eclipse. I expect Mossdeep's fuller season of offensive production to prevail, but Rustboro has a route through a balanced attack that keeps Marino waiting and makes the depleted secondary defend several different answers. Tyler Scarboro cannot let another receiving performance become as uncontested as the box-score totals suggest Vermilion's was. Michael Dorrill cannot assume last week's four touchdown catches will travel as a standing appointment.
matchups.awayKey: Gain at least 350 total yards and commit no more than one turnover.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least 140 yards and hold Mossdeep below four offensive touchdowns.

matchups.matchup: Petalburg can make modest passing totals work
matchups.analysis: The Pride beat Pewter 24–17 with 115 passing yards from Iron Valiant, two touchdown throws and useful running support. Oinkologne scored on the ground and through the air. Petalburg is 7–3; Sootopolis is 4–6 after losing 24–14 to Fuchsia. Drampa completed eleven of twenty-seven, a sharp change from the clean performance that beat Vermilion. I expect Norman's team to keep finding enough ordinary gains to control the scoring pace. The Surge can challenge that by protecting Drampa and making Arbok's receiving opportunities count before the game becomes a sequence of obvious passing downs. Heatmor remains out at tight end. Wallace needs the version of his passing game that completes drives, not another alternating week of competence and explanation.
matchups.awayKey: Complete at least sixty percent of passes and allow no more than two sacks.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least one hundred yards and score on four possessions.

matchups.matchup: Dewford tries to keep the late drama optional
matchups.analysis: The Breakers won 16–10 at Celadon, with Frosmoth completing fourteen of twenty for two hundred yards and a touchdown. At 6–4, Dewford occupies the seventh seed in its conference's current table. Lavaridge is 4–6 after winning 22–21 at Cerulean, a second straight victory that makes the Inferno more than a soft entry on the schedule. Stantler is now out two weeks, complicating the visitors' rushing plan. I favor Dewford because its recent passing has been steadier, while Lavaridge's defense still allowed 321 yards through the air in the win. Flannery's team can make this uncomfortable if Delphox keeps producing touchdowns and the defense makes the Breakers settle for kicks. Brawly should treat a narrow favorite's role as a responsibility, not an excuse to wait until the last possession.
matchups.awayKey: Allow fewer than 250 passing yards and score at least two passing touchdowns.
matchups.homeKey: Finish three touchdown drives and lose no turnovers.

matchups.matchup: Fortree has to begin again after fifty-two to nothing
matchups.analysis: The Skyhawks' three-game recovery ended in a 52–0 loss at Saffron. Rabsca threw for 145 yards and no touchdowns, while Pawmot joined the injury list for six weeks. Fortree is 3–7; Mauville returns from its bye at 4–6 after beating Celadon 24–6. Togekiss threw for 238 yards in that game, with Mothim catching eight passes. I favor the Dynamos because that established receiving route can test a defense whose latest afternoon offered little resistance. The danger for Wattson is assuming the score at Saffron describes every Fortree possession to come. Winona still has useful rushing options and Ariados back without a remaining absence. The Skyhawks need a functional opening series and several more like it, with fewer demands placed on a defense still absorbing the last result.

matchups.matchup: Pastoria’s two wins have come through different kinds of offense
matchups.analysis: Togekiss threw for 230 yards in Pastoria's win over Lavender and 105 in its 20–13 win at Mahogany. Both counted. Watchog #58's seventy-seven rushing yards helped the second result, and the Waves have reached 4–6. Oreburgh is 3–8 after beating Azalea 13–10, with Cryogonal throwing two touchdowns and an interception. I take Pastoria because its recent defense and its ability to find different sources of movement look slightly more dependable. Arbok is now out four weeks, however, and Oinkologne remains absent three. Roark's team can take advantage if Diggersby's running forces the Waves to defend long possessions while their own receiving options adjust. Neither side has enough scoring cushion to treat a giveaway as an acceptable cost of doing business.

matchups.matchup: Sunyshore reaches a second consecutive road examination
matchups.analysis: The Starseekers beat Blackthorn 21–20 behind 146 rushing yards and two touchdowns from FLOAT SZN. At 8–2, they visit an Eterna side that fell to 6–4 after losing 38–0 at Mt. Silver. Tatsugiri completed eight of nineteen for forty-one yards. I expect Sunyshore to make the Thorns produce a much broader offensive answer before the home defense can decide the game. Myles Gabite remains out two weeks, but the latest rushing performance showed a useful way to carry the workload. Eterna's response begins with Stantler, who had forty-one rushing yards after the previous week's 140. Gardenia needs early-down gains that keep the quarterback from facing the entire repair job. The Thorns' earlier defensive work still deserves respect; it needs points to support it.

matchups.matchup: Two teams need a productive afternoon to survive its mistakes
matchups.analysis: Snowpoint lost 17–7 at Cianwood despite Drampa completing twenty-three passes for 201 yards. Veilstone lost 31–14 at Lavender, with Tatsugiri completing ten of twenty-eight and throwing two interceptions. The Blizzard are 2–8 and the Fists 4–7. I take Veilstone by the smallest useful margin because Vigoroth's sixty rushing yards offered a foundation its passing game failed to use. Candice's team can reverse that call by making its more frequent completions produce touchdowns. Maylene needs the defense to recover from Lavender's 101-yard Diggersby game and give her offense fewer long scoring assignments. This is not a forecast of polished football. It is a bet that the visitors can remove one damaging mistake before Snowpoint fixes its finishing.

articles.title: Three scoreboards stand between Mossdeep and Hoenn East
articles.dek: Mossdeep can secure Hoenn East; Mt. Silver can book a playoff place. Ellis Quill lays out every Week 12 clinching combination and the games shaping both brackets.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: I generally distrust the moment a season starts looking finished on a standings page. The clubs below the line still have games to play, and the clubs above it still have opponents who would enjoy spoiling an afternoon. But Week 12 gives Mossdeep something firmer than a flattering seed: a route to securing Hoenn East. Ten wins have bought the Eclipse that opportunity. They have not yet bought the division, a first-round rest or an appointment in the Indigo Bowl.

Michael Dorrill’s team is 10–0 after beating Vermilion 45–21. Sootopolis and Lavaridge are both 4–6, while Fortree is 3–7. Seven games remain for all four clubs. The distance looks enormous because it is enormous. It also leaves a little arithmetic to do before anybody orders the celebratory banner.
Mossdeep’s two division-clinching routes

Under the league’s published playoff rules, the first route requires a Mossdeep victory at Rustboro, plus Sootopolis failing to win at Petalburg and Lavaridge failing to win at Dewford. A loss or a tie is sufficient for each pursuer. All three parts matter. A Mossdeep win by itself would take the Eclipse to 11–0, but a victorious Sootopolis or Lavaridge could still finish with 11 wins by taking its remaining six games.

The second route begins with a Mossdeep–Rustboro tie. In that case, both Sootopolis and Lavaridge must lose. Mossdeep would have ten wins and a tie, worth ten and a half wins in the standings even if it lost its last six games. Those two rivals would each be capped at ten wins. Fortree can already finish with no more than ten, so it cannot interfere with either of these clinching combinations.

If Mossdeep loses, Hoenn East remains unsettled through this round. And if the Eclipse win while either principal pursuer also wins, an equal final record is still possible. The division tiebreaks cannot simply be waved away: a pursuer that wins out also improves its division record, while a Mossdeep collapse would damage its own. The six-game lead does real work here, but it does not make every equal-record finish safe.

Those are the complete Week 12 combinations for securing Hoenn East. There is also a separate route to clinching a playoff berth while leaving the division open: Mossdeep wins; Sootopolis, Lavaridge and Sunyshore all win; Mauville fails to beat Fortree; and Pastoria fails to beat Oreburgh. A tie satisfies either of those last two requirements. Every part is required for this additional route. The results squeeze the remaining wild-card competition enough for Mossdeep’s head-to-head wins and the ordering of the other contenders to protect a place even in a late-season collapse.
The road after Rustboro still matters

A division title would settle one argument and leave several others open. Mossdeep’s remaining itinerary is Rustboro away, Fortree away, Petalburg at home, Canalave away, Sunyshore at home, Sootopolis at home and Lavaridge away. The Eclipse have to cross three of the conference’s present playoff positions in successive games from Weeks 14 through 16. Petalburg is the third seed, Canalave the fourth and Sunyshore the second. That is a fairly persuasive objection to treating November as a victory lap.

Sunyshore’s visit in Week 16 is the obvious appointment in the race for the conference’s first seed. The Starseekers are 8–2 after their 21–20 escape at Blackthorn. Before Mossdeep, they travel to Eterna and Hearthome, then host Canalave and Rustboro. If Sunyshore keeps winning while Mossdeep drops games, that meeting can become a direct opportunity to change the order at the top. If the Eclipse keep winning, the same fixture becomes a much steeper chase. Those are conditional paths, not an announcement that either club has secured the bye.

Only the first seed in each conference rests during the wild-card round. Nobody can secure that privilege through Week 12. Even an Eclipse win leaves enough schedule for Sunyshore to finish above a Mossdeep team that subsequently loses out. I would still make Mossdeep my first-seed choice today. A forecast can have a favorite without pretending the remaining six games have already happened.
Mt. Silver’s lead has a different shape

Across the league, Connor McLarren’s Mt. Silver Reds are also 10–0, with 277 points scored and only 68 conceded. Their 38–0 win over Eterna did nothing to make the defense look charitable. They now host 8–2 Blackthorn, the current second seed in Kanto–Johto, in a game that reaches well beyond the Reds’ immediate neighborhood.

Mt. Silver cannot clinch Johto West this week, even with a win and an Olivine loss. That combination would leave the Reds with an 11-win floor and the Ironclads with an 11-win ceiling. Olivine could reach that ceiling by winning out, including its Week 13 trip to Mt. Silver, and take the division tiebreak in that particular finish. It is an unlikely-looking road when one watches the Reds play. It is still an open road in the standings.

The Reds can, however, secure a playoff berth this week. They must beat Blackthorn, Olivine must beat Violet, Cianwood must beat Lavender, and Cerulean must fail to beat Celadon. Then one of two additional combinations is needed: Vermilion and Viridian tie; or Vermilion wins and Pewter fails to beat Fuchsia. A Cerulean tie is sufficient, and a Pewter tie is sufficient in that second branch. The Saffron–Cinnabar and Azalea–Mahogany results do not affect those combinations. It is a longer shopping list than Mossdeep’s division route, but it can deliver a postseason place without settling Johto West.

McLarren’s remaining opponents are Blackthorn, Olivine, Mahogany, Saffron, Cinnabar, Azalea and Cianwood. Saffron’s Week 15 visit and Mt. Silver’s Week 16 trip to Cinnabar put two current division leaders directly in the Reds’ path. The Psi Corps, now 8–2 after beating Fortree 52–0, go to 7–3 Cinnabar this week. A Saffron win keeps pressure on the conference leaders and damages Cinnabar’s margin in Kanto West. A Blaze win pulls those two clubs level at eight victories. Neither result comes with a first-round bye attached.
The seventh seed has neighbors

The present Hoenn–Sinnoh order is Mossdeep, Sunyshore, Petalburg, Canalave, Rustboro, Eterna and Dewford. If those positions survived to the postseason, the opening games would be Sunyshore–Dewford, Petalburg–Eterna and Canalave–Rustboro, with Mossdeep waiting. They are a picture of the current bracket, not scheduled playoff fixtures. Canalave has played 11 games and is 7–4; the three current wild-card clubs are all 6–4. The Bulwark’s Week 12 bye makes that difference in games played especially visible.

Rustboro’s immediate task is difficult and useful: beat the unbeaten visitors, then keep moving through a schedule that includes Sunyshore, Canalave, Petalburg and Dewford. Those last two divisional meetings arrive in Weeks 17 and 18. Petalburg already leads Hoenn West at 7–3, and its Week 13 home game against Dewford precedes the trip to Mossdeep. A Pride stumble can help both six-win pursuers; their remaining head-to-head games ensure that nobody gets to improve every contender’s record at once.

Eterna and Canalave meet in Week 13. First, the Thorns host Sunyshore after losing 38–0 at Mt. Silver. An Eterna win would repair its own position and help Mossdeep’s first-seed chase; a loss would give Rustboro and Dewford an opportunity to move ahead in wins. The standings are full of favors that nobody intends to perform.

Kanto–Johto currently lines up Mt. Silver, Blackthorn, Saffron, Cinnabar, Vermilion, Violet and Lavender. Hold those seeds and the wild-card games would be Blackthorn–Lavender, Saffron–Violet and Cinnabar–Vermilion. Lavender’s 31–14 win over Veilstone has brought the Wails to 5–5 and seventh place, level in record with Olivine immediately outside the bracket. Travis Scarboro’s club goes to Cianwood while Violet visits Olivine. That second game guarantees dropped standing ground for at least one of Lavender’s nearby rivals; the Wails still have to take care of their own trip.

No club has yet secured a playoff berth. The first item I will be checking this week is therefore wonderfully specific: Mossdeep’s result at Rustboro, Sootopolis’s result at Petalburg and Lavaridge’s result at Dewford. Three scoreboards can turn Hoenn East from a commanding lead into a finished race. The rest of the conference would still have plenty to discuss.
